title: Giving Both Sides of a Debate

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *aunque* from A2 Unit 28, and *sin embargo* and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1. A debate about the Maya Train needs both: you grant one side's point and then give the other. *Aunque* joins two clauses in one sentence; *sin embargo* and *no obstante* start a new sentence or clause.

sections.title: Three ways to give the other side
rows: Aunque el tren crea empleos, algunas comunidades lo critican.
*aunque* + indicative in one sentence (although the train creates jobs, some communities criticise it)
El tren crea empleos; sin embargo, algunas comunidades lo critican.
*sin embargo* after a semicolon or full stop (however)
El tren crea empleos. No obstante, algunas comunidades lo critican.

items.spanish: Aunque la milpa necesita mucho trabajo, muchas familias la siguen sembrando.
items.english: Although the milpa needs a lot of work, many families keep planting it.

items.spanish: El Gobierno defiende el tren; sin embargo, algunos científicos temen por los cenotes.
items.english: The government defends the train; however, some scientists fear for the cenotes.

items.spanish: El tren llega a sitios arqueológicos. No obstante, algunas comunidades piden más consultas.
items.english: The train reaches archaeological sites. Nevertheless, some communities ask for more consultations.

items.spanish: Aunque el maíz es la base de la milpa, también se siembran frijol y calabaza.
items.english: Although maize is the base of the milpa, beans and squash are also planted.

sections.content: *Sin embargo* and *no obstante* are followed by a comma. *Aunque* can come first or second: *aunque el tren crea empleos, algunas comunidades lo critican* means the same as *algunas comunidades lo critican aunque el tren crea empleos*.
